name: Battle of Okinawa
info: United States Army and Marine Corps forces invaded Okinawa on 1 April 1945 and, after 82 days against the Japanese Thirty-Second Army, took the island at a cost that fell most heavily on its Okinawan civilians.

facts.date: 1 April to 22 June 1945, after the capture of the Kerama Islands on 26 March; mopping-up ran to 30 June
facts.place: The island of Okinawa and the seas and islands around it, in the Ryukyu Islands, present-day Japan
facts.sides: The United States Tenth Army under Lieutenant General Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr., with 182,821 personnel at the start, supported by a fleet and by British Task Force 57; the Japanese Thirty-Second Army under Lieutenant General Mitsuru Ushijima, about 100,000 troops at the onset, including drafted Okinawans
facts.outcome: The Americans took the island. The Japanese Thirty-Second Army was destroyed, its commanders died by suicide, and Okinawa became a fleet anchorage and airfield base close to Japan.

t: The Okinawan civilian dead are counted differently by different bodies: at least 149,425 killed, dead by coerced suicide or missing by the local authorities' count, and about 42,000 non-uniformed civilians by the US Tenth Army's, and the figures are not reconciled.
The Japanese Thirty-Second Army fought a defensive battle from fortified caves and reverse slopes, and for the first time kamikaze attacks became a major institutionalised part of Japan's defence.

Civilians were used as human shields, had food taken from them, and were urged to kill themselves and their families; the extent of the army's role in the mass suicides is still disputed between Okinawa and Japan's national government.
dyk: The Japanese army mobilised 1,780 schoolboys aged 14 to 17 into front-line service, and female students into a nursing unit; about half of the boys were killed.
ev: The US 77th Infantry Division takes the Kerama Islands west of Okinawa
The Tenth Army lands on the Hagushi beaches and takes the Kadena and Yomitan airbases within hours
About 400 Japanese planes attack from Kyushu on 6 April, and the battleship Yamato sails on a suicide attack and is sunk
The Thirty-Second Army attacks across the whole front on three nights and is repulsed
The 96th Infantry Division takes Conical Hill, and the Marines fight for Sugar Loaf Hill
Marines occupy Shuri Castle after the Japanese withdraw south
General Buckner is killed by Japanese artillery fire
The last Japanese resistance ends and Ushijima and Chō die by suicide

sections.background:
By early 1945 the Allies had advanced across the Pacific by island hopping. They planned to use Kadena Air Base on Okinawa as a staging point for Operation Downfall, the planned invasion of the Japanese home islands, 340 miles (550 km) away. Okinawa was the largest amphibious assault of the Pacific Theater. Before the main landing, the 77th Infantry Division captured the Kerama Islands on 26 March, which gave the fleet a protected anchorage and removed the threat from suicide boats.

The Japanese expected the Americans to land six to ten divisions against a garrison of two and a half divisions. Their staff calculated that, with superior weapons, each American division had five or six times the firepower of a Japanese division, to which the Americans would add abundant naval and air firepower. The 9th Division was moved to Taiwan before the invasion, which forced a reshuffle of the defensive plans.

Within the Thirty-Second Army, Colonel Hiromichi Yahara advocated a defensive strategy and Lieutenant General Isamu Chō an offensive one. The Japanese had used kamikaze tactics since the Battle of Leyte Gulf, but at Okinawa they became a major institutionalised part of the defence. Okinawa was also home to a large civilian population, which US planners assumed numbered about 300,000.
sections.forces:
The Americans formed the Tenth Army, a cross-branch force of the 7th, 27th, 77th and 96th Infantry Divisions and the 1st, 2nd and 6th Marine Divisions, with its own Tactical Air Force. It had 182,821 personnel at the start, under Lieutenant General Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr. The invasion was supported by 18 battleships, 27 cruisers, 177 destroyers and destroyer escorts and 39 aircraft carriers, and over 3,000 aircraft were provided over the battle. A British Commonwealth fleet with Australian, New Zealand and Canadian ships served as Task Force 57.

The Japanese land campaign, mainly defensive, was fought by the 32nd Army of 67,000 men (77,000 according to some sources), under Lieutenant General Mitsuru Ushijima, and some 9,000 naval troops at Oroku under Rear Admiral Minoru Ōta, only a few hundred of them trained for ground combat. They were supported by 39,000 drafted Ryukyuan people: 24,000 hastily drafted militia called Boeitai and 15,000 non-uniformed labourers. Colonel Takehiko Udo commanded in the north.

The army also mobilised 1,780 schoolboys aged 14 to 17 as the Iron and Blood Imperial Corps, while female Himeyuri students were organised into a nursing unit. The mobilisation was by ordinance of the Ministry of the Army, not by law. The students were nominally volunteers, but the authorities ordered schools to make almost all of them volunteer, sometimes with forged documents. About half of the corps were killed, among the 2,000 students of 21 schools who died on the battlefield.
sections.course:
On 28 March, 394 civilians on Tokashiki island were forced by Japanese soldiers to kill themselves after US troops landed. The main landing came on 1 April on the Hagushi beaches on the west coast, and the Tenth Army took the Kadena and Yomitan airbases within hours against weak opposition. The 6th Marine Division sealed off the Motobu Peninsula by 7 April and cleared Mount Yaedake on 18 April, and the 77th Infantry Division took Ie Shima between 16 and 21 April. At sea, about 400 Japanese planes attacked from Kyushu on 6 April, and the battleship Yamato and five other warships were sunk on their way to Okinawa.

In the south the Japanese fought from fortified caves on the Shuri Line, with defences on reverse slopes. The advance on Kakazu Ridge was costly, and the Japanese sent Okinawans out at gunpoint to fetch water and supplies, which led to civilian casualties. The Thirty-Second Army counter-attacked on the nights of 12 to 14 April and again on 4 May, and both attacks failed. On 19 April the Americans fired a barrage of 324 guns, the largest in the Pacific Theater. Conical Hill fell on 13 May, and Sugar Loaf Hill was fought for at the same time. Monsoon rains turned the field to mud.

The Japanese withdrew by night from Shuri, and Marines entered the castle on 29 May. Nearly 30,000 personnel reached the Kiyan Peninsula. In June the naval troops at Oroku died by suicide in their tunnels on 13 June. General Buckner was killed on 18 June and organised resistance ended on 21 June, when Ushijima and Chō died by seppuku.
sections.aftermath:
The Americans suffered some 48,000 casualties, not counting some 33,000 non-battle casualties, and over 12,000 were killed or missing. At sea, 36 Allied ships were sunk and 368 damaged. The US military estimates that 110,071 Japanese soldiers were killed, a total that includes conscripted Okinawans. 7,401 Japanese regulars and 3,400 Okinawan conscripts were captured or surrendered during the battle, and 16,346 in all by later months.

The civilian losses were of another order. The US Tenth Army counted 142,058 enemy bodies, including civilians pressed into service, and deduced that about 42,000 were non-uniformed civilians killed in the crossfire. Okinawa Prefecture estimates over 100,000 losses, and the local authorities say at least 149,425 Okinawans were killed, died by coerced suicide or went missing. 40,000 of those killed had been drafted or impressed by the Japanese army and are often counted as combat deaths.

The Okinawa Prefectural Peace Memorial Museum says the Japanese army showed indifference to Okinawans' safety, used civilians as human shields or killed them, confiscated food and executed those who hid it, leading to mass starvation, and forced civilians out of shelters. Japanese soldiers killed about 1,000 people who spoke the Okinawan language, to suppress spying. Civilians in the south also killed their families and themselves, urged on by soldiers who said the Americans would kill and rape them. At least 90% of the buildings on the island were destroyed.
sections.sources:
The most complete tally of deaths is the Cornerstone of Peace monument at the Okinawa Prefectural Peace Memorial Museum, which lists each person by name: 242,046 names as of 2023, including 149,634 Okinawans, 77,823 Imperial Japanese soldiers and 14,010 Americans. It also counts Okinawan deaths over a longer period than the battle, from the Manchurian Incident to a year after the surrender, so its totals cannot be read as the battle's alone.

Official counts and local ones differ, and the Okinawan civilian toll depends on whether conscripted Okinawans are counted as civilians or as combatants. Early claims of Japanese aircraft lost, 7,800, were not borne out by later examination of Japanese records, which put the loss at roughly 1,430. The Ryūkyū Shimpō wrote in 2007 that many Okinawans testified that the Japanese army directed them to commit suicide, and some that they were handed grenades. Colonel Yahara, the most senior officer to survive, wrote The Battle for Okinawa.

Witnesses and historians claim that American and Japanese soldiers raped Okinawan women. Marine Corps officials said they knew of no rapes by American personnel, but there are numerous credible testimonies that many were committed by Americans.
sections.legacy:
Historians have judged the battle differently. Hanson W. Baldwin wrote that never before had the Navy lost so many ships, and that the American casualties were the highest in any campaign against the Japanese. Some military historians, among them Victor Davis Hanson, believe the campaign led directly to the atomic bombings, as a means of avoiding an invasion of the Japanese mainland. Others debate why Japan surrendered, citing the bombings, the Soviet invasion of Manchuria and depleted resources. The United States then set up the United States Civil Administration of the Ryukyu Islands, a military government.

The civilian suicides remain disputed. In March 2007 Japan's education ministry (MEXT) advised textbook publishers to reword descriptions saying that the army forced civilians to kill themselves. On 29 September 2007 about 110,000 people rallied in Okinawa in protest. In December 2007 the ministry's council allowed the wording that civilians were forced into mass suicides by the military, with context. In March 2008 the Osaka court ruled for Kenzaburō Ōe, who had been sued over his statement that the military ordered them, saying the military was deeply involved.

In 1995 the Okinawa government erected the Cornerstone of Peace at Mabuni, which lists all the known dead, civilian and military, Japanese and foreign. It listed 242,225 names as of 2024. Kadena remains the largest US air base in Asia, and local residents have long protested against the size and presence of the bases.

summary: The Battle of Okinawa, from 1 April to 22 June 1945, was the largest amphibious assault of the Pacific War. The Americans took the island, the Japanese Thirty-Second Army was destroyed, and at least 149,425 Okinawans were killed, died by coerced suicide or went missing.

notes: Civilian figures: the article gives 149,425 (local authorities), over 100,000 (prefecture), 142,058 bodies with about 42,000 civilians (Tenth Army) and the Cornerstone's 149,634 Okinawans, over a longer period; I gave each with its owner and did not reconcile them. The article's own first-paragraph phrase is 'at least 149,425 Okinawan people were killed, died by coerced suicide or went missing' per local authorities.

The article gives 'about 81 days' in the land battle and '82-day battle' in the lead; I used the dates only. Allied/Japanese casualty overview in the lead (50,000 Allied, around 100,000 Japanese) is not repeated; the aftermath gives the detailed figures.
Aftermath figure of Americans: 'some 48,000 casualties, not including some 33,000 non-battle'; the article notes Keegan has higher numbers, left out for length.

Left out: the mental breakdown quotation from the Marine Corps Gazette, the infantryman's quotation about firing on houses, the Confederate flag at Shuri, the Medal of Honor list, Pyle, the detail of ship losses and carriers, Operation Gi-gou, the Katsuyama vigilante story, Feifer and the Guardian official's quotation, Mitscher's flagships.
The article says the Cornerstone's total as 242,046 (2023) in Casualties and 242,225 (2024) in Memorial; I gave each with its year.
The article contradicts itself on Allied naval: 'no major Allied warship was lost' yet 36 ships sunk; I gave only the 36 and 368 figures.
The textbook section says MEXT 'partially admitted'; I wrote that the council allowed the wording with context.
Hanson quotation is paraphrased; it ends with '[unconditionally]' in brackets in the article.
